finding.claim: authorize() is async but not awaited in DELETE /reports/:id, so the authorization check is not enforced. Any authenticated user can delete any report. The rejected promise is also unhandled, which can crash the process on Node 15+ or leave an unhandled rejection.
finding.source: Authenticated user supplies req.params.id of a report they have no 'delete' grant on

trace.note: authorize() called without await; the returned Promise is discarded and execution continues
grants lookup and 403 throw occur asynchronously, after the handler has moved on

finding.guards_checked: authorize() would throw 403 if awaited. The PUT route awaits it correctly, so the DELETE route lacks the guard. No other middleware enforces authorization; the only global middleware copies req.session.user.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws 403 on missing grant, but the DELETE handler calls it without await (line 20), so the result is discarded. The only global middleware (lines 4-7) copies the session user and enforces nothing. No other control found.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls async authorize() as a bare statement, so line 21 db.reports.remove runs regardless of the grant check, unlike the PUT route's `await` at line 27. Any authenticated user can therefore delete any report.

finding.claim: Mass assignment in PUT /reports/:id: the whole request body is passed to db.reports.update, so a caller with write access to a report can set protected fields such as owner_id, tenant_id or id. This could move or reassign a report, or change ownership or grants. The impact depends on the db schema, which is not in the repo.
finding.source: req.body (JSON) from a user with 'write' grant on the report

trace.note: express.json() parses an arbitrary JSON body
unfiltered body is passed to update

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist or schema validation. The authorize check covers only the write action and does not restrict which fields may be written.

verdict.guard_found: authorize (server.js:9-16) throws 403 if the 'write' grant is missing and is awaited at line 27, so it is effective for access. No field allowlist, schema validation or body filtering exists.
verdict.reason: server.js:28 passes the unfiltered req.body (parsed at server.js:3) to db.reports.update after only the awaited 'write' grant check at server.js:27, so a low-privilege writer can set protected fields. The impact depends on the db schema, which is not in the repo.

finding.claim: The auth middleware does not reject unauthenticated requests. req.user = req.session.user is set without checking that a session or user exists, and no session middleware is registered in this file. If a session exists without a user, req.user is undefined and authorize() throws a TypeError on user.id. That gives a 500 or unhandled rejection rather than a clean 401. In the DELETE route the throw is in the un-awaited promise, so an unauthenticated request still deletes the report. This is a lower-confidence variant of finding 1.

trace.note: authorize() rejects with a TypeError, but the promise is not awaited

finding.guards_checked: No 401 guard on any route. express-session is not configured in this file; it may exist elsewhere, but only server.js is present.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws on a missing grant or missing user, but the DELETE route at server.js:20 calls it without await, so the rejection is never observed. No 401 guard exists, and no session middleware is registered in this file.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so a rejection (TypeError from user.id at server.js:10 when req.user is undefined from server.js:5) is discarded and db.reports.remove runs at server.js:21; this assumes session middleware exists elsewhere, since otherwise server.js:5 throws first and every request fails.
